strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: Clear demonstration (Figure 2) of why existing training-free motion customization fails on distilled models due to coarse denoising and mismatched behavior
Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple metrics, cross-model generalization, user study with 50 participants, and detailed ablations (Tables 3-7)
Practical efficiency: Achieves competitive quality in 6-13 seconds with clear speed-quality tradeoffs across different step counts
Successful generalization: Demonstrated on multiple distilled models (T2V-Turbo-V2, AnimateDiff-Lightning) and integrates with different motion guidance approaches
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with effective visualizations of motion representations and method overview
Ethical awareness: Thoughtful discussion of potential misuse and proposed safeguards
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Core components are existing techniques—test-time distillation with score-based supervision (standard), motion guidance via temporal attention (from MotionClone), noise initialization (from prior works). Main contribution is their combination for distilled models, which is primarily an engineering contribution

Excessive hyperparameter complexity: 9+ hyperparameters (δ₁, δ₂, λ, η, k, τ, W, N_max) with motion-type-dependent tuning; grid search selection suggests sensitivity; no principled method for new scenarios

Ad-hoc design choices: Moving-window criterion, dynamic truncation threshold, and fixed τ for motion guidance proportion lack theoretical justification; appear empirically motivated rather than principled
Missing computational cost analysis: Algorithm 1 shows nested teacher denoising but provides no breakdown of teacher vs. student time; net overhead (~2s) not thoroughly analyzed
Limited benchmark scale: TurboBench has only 66 pairs from 22 videos; AnimateBench is very small (15 videos); insufficient for robust generalization claims
Incomplete ablation studies: No ablation on τ (critical parameter), sensitivity analysis for thresholds incomplete, failure modes not discussed
Metric limitations: Motion Fidelity relies on potentially unreliable Co-Tracker trajectories; temporal consistency via CLIP embeddings may miss artifacts; FID selection criteria undefined
Reproducibility concerns: Code not available at review, 9+ hyperparameters requiring scenario-specific tuning, incomplete sensitivity analysis
Oversensitivity to noise initialization: Blend factor k varies significantly by motion type (0.01-0.3 across scenarios); justification for values superficial
User study gaps: No inter-rater agreement reported; win rates often modest (43-53% vs. 15-16%); online survey format may introduce quality variance

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies and demonstrates the fundamental incompatibility between existing motion customization methods and distilled video generators, addressing a practically important gap

Comprehensive experimental validation: extensive testing across multiple distilled models (T2V-Turbo-V2, Wan2.1-1.3B, Video-Blade, CogVideoX-2B), diverse benchmarks (TurboBench, DavisBench, LOVEU-TGVE), rich metrics, thorough ablations, and user study
Elegant technical solution: teacher-guided trajectory correction via score interpolation is mathematically sound and directly addresses the sparse denoising dynamics problem of distilled models

Practical framework: training-free approach without model retraining, architecture-agnostic design, extends to multiple motion representation types (MOFT, DVIT, DITFlow), and works with different guidance strategies

Excellent presentation and reproducibility: clear writing, detailed algorithm pseudo-code (Algorithm 1), extensive implementation details in appendices, and honest discussion of limitations and failure cases
Thoughtful ethical considerations: Section E addresses potential misuse, data provenance concerns, and commits to open-sourcing code for collaborative safety research
weaknesses: Incremental technical novelty: while the overall framework is novel, individual components are applications of existing techniques (score interpolation, adaptive guidance scheduling) without substantial innovation per component

Computational overhead contradicts efficiency motivation: 2x-4x increase in inference time (7s→13s for TurboV2, 33s→55s for VB, Tables 12) significantly limits practical adoption for speed-critical applications, undermining the fast generation premise
Modest improvements on key metrics: Motion Fidelity gains often ~2-3% absolute improvement, some Text Alignment improvements are incremental; fundamental gap vs. full models remains

Methodological concerns about claims: 'training-free' is misleading (requires pre-trained teacher); multiple hyperparameters (λ, η, δ₁, δ₂, W) contradict ease-of-use narrative; no sensitivity analysis provided despite empirical hyperparameter tuning
Limited experimental rigor: user study with 50 participants lacks statistical significance testing; no experiments varying teacher quality; scope limited to T2V domain with unclear generalization

Theoretical justification gaps: adaptive acceleration strategy (Sec. 3.4) is ad-hoc without principled justification; method fundamentally constrained by teacher model quality without thorough investigation of this dependency
Acknowledged but unresolved failure modes: fine-grained motion control limitations (Fig. 8) remain, restricting applicability to complex scenarios and detailed motion types
Presentation issues: inconsistent notation in equations, critical baseline details relegated to appendices, connection between motion loss formulation and trajectory correction could be clearer

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies a real practical limitation where existing motion customization methods fail on distilled video generators

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive evaluation across multiple benchmarks (TurboBench, DavisBench, LOVEU-TGVE, AnimateBench) and diverse model architectures with thorough ablation studies
Solid technical execution: Sound mathematical formulation with well-justified teacher-guided trajectory correction approach and adaptive acceleration strategy
Detailed computational analysis: Includes GPU memory, inference time, and practical overhead comparisons demonstrating realistic cost-benefit tradeoffs
Thorough evaluation methodology: User studies, multiple metrics, diverse motion patterns, and both quantitative and qualitative results
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: Core solution relies on combining existing techniques (score distillation, classifier-free guidance, teacher-student guidance) without significant new algorithmic insights

Self-defeating solution: Requires loading full teacher model at inference (doubling memory usage and nearly doubling inference time), largely negating computational benefits of distillation and raising question of why not simply use the full model
Unclear practical utility: No clear guidance on when practitioners should use this approach versus simply using the full teacher model for motion customization directly

Questionable generalization: Limited analysis of transferability to future distilled models with different distillation strategies, architectures, or scales; hyperparameter generalization strategy unclear
Hyperparameter complexity: Introduces multiple hyperparameters (λ, η, δ₁, δ₂, W, timestep schedule) with limited guidance for setting on new models; incomplete sensitivity analysis
Missing comparative analyses: No comparison with alternative solutions like fine-tuning distilled models, distillation strategies that preserve motion, or other architectural approaches

Presentation issues: Title is misleading (distillation doesn't fundamentally 'break' motion control); dense notation with inconsistencies; key algorithmic details relegated to appendix; 48-page length is unnecessarily long
Limited scope: Method is specific to motion customization; applicability to other downstream tasks or uses of distilled models is unexplored
Failure case analysis: Acknowledges limitations for scenarios with structural discrepancy (Figure 8) but provides insufficient solutions or deeper analysis

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies and demonstrates how existing motion customization methods fail on distilled video generators due to collapsed denoising trajectories—a genuine limitation at the intersection of knowledge distillation and motion control.

Technically sound and novel solution: Teacher-guided trajectory correction with adaptive acceleration strategy is mathematically principled and creative. The adaptive scheduling mechanism that monitors motion loss to dynamically decide teacher guidance is particularly elegant.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive evaluation across multiple distilled models (T2V-Turbo-V2, Video-Blade, Wan2.1, CogVideoX-2B), three benchmarks (TurboBench, DavisBench, LOVEU-TGVE), multiple metrics, ablation studies, and user study with 50 participants. Computational analysis demonstrates practical feasibility.

Architecture-agnostic design: Method works with different motion extractors (MotionClone, MotionDirector, MOFT, DMVT) and diffusion backbones, demonstrating genuine generality and practical applicability.

Excellent presentation and reproducibility: Clear problem visualization, well-organized methodology with intuitive pipeline diagram, complete algorithmic description (Algorithm 1), extensive hyperparameter documentation, and commitment to release code. Mathematical derivations are rigorous.

Practical value without retraining: Training-free approach enables efficient motion control on existing distilled models without requiring model retraining or fine-tuning, making it immediately applicable.

Meaningful limitations discussion: Acknowledges shortcomings (object-motion misalignment, fine-grained control), discusses future work directions, and includes thoughtful treatment of ethical concerns regarding misuse potential.
weaknesses: Teacher model dependency at inference: Requires access to full, non-distilled teacher model during inference, limiting applicability when teachers are unavailable, proprietary, or resource-constrained. Offline caching of teacher guidance is not explored.

Limited failure case analysis: While one failure case is shown (Figure 8), systematic analysis of failure modes is lacking. Questions remain about when adaptive scheduling incorrectly terminates guidance, which motion types are challenging, and degradation with minimal teacher steps.

Inference cost remains substantial: TurboV2 requires 7-13s (vs. 7s baseline) and Video-Blade requires 23-55s (vs. ~20s baseline). For a method targeting 'fast' generators, this overhead is meaningful and could use more thorough discussion of quality-speed trade-offs.

Limited exploration of out-of-distribution motions: All experiments use natural reference videos. Method is not evaluated on synthesized motions, extreme camera movements, physically impossible transitions, or other creative scenarios that may appear in real applications.

Hyperparameter tuning guidance: While ablations show robustness (Tables 4-5), practical guidance for setting λ, η, δ₁, δ₂, W, N_min on new datasets/models is limited. Sensitivity analysis focuses primarily on TurboV2.

Fixed score interpolation weight: Equation 5 uses constant interpolation weight to control guidance strength—a somewhat simplistic approach. Adaptive weighting per timestep might improve quality-efficiency trade-off.
User study design details: 50 participants is adequate, but inter-rater agreement metrics and statistical significance testing details would strengthen perceptual quality claims.
